note: Curriculum scenarios and qualitative reviewer criteria; not verified assessment results.

tracks.title: Isolated lab outage and recovery
tracks.brief: A fictional company training lab has a Windows VM, Linux service VM, internal DNS VM, and an offline hypervisor. After changes to a virtual switch, the Windows VM can no longer open the internal application. All systems are owned by your lab; no production network access is authorized.

stages.title: Establish scope and baseline
stages.evidence: Host RAM 16 GB, host use 5 GB, Windows guest 6 GB, Linux guest 4 GB, DNS guest 2 GB. Virtual switch changed from host-only to bridged at 14:05. No external network connectivity is part of the approved lab scope.
stages.prompt: Calculate the requested memory budget and headroom. Name two safety concerns, record what must not be tested, and describe the first reversible action.
stages.tools: Linux host: free -h; ip -br addr; ip route. Windows guest: Get-NetAdapter; Get-NetIPConfiguration.
stages.interpret: Guest memory requests total 12 GB and host use adds 5 GB = 17 GB, exceeding 16 GB before overhead. Bridged networking may violate isolation. Inspect before changing anything.
criteria: Correct memory arithmetic and overhead caveat
Clear authorized scope and isolation boundary
At least two relevant command outputs described

stages.title: Differentiate failure modes
stages.evidence: Windows VM has 10.40.0.22/24 and gateway 10.40.0.1. Linux service is 10.40.0.80; DNS is 10.40.0.53. Ping to gateway succeeds. `Resolve-DnsName app.lab.example -Server 10.40.0.53` times out. `Test-NetConnection 10.40.0.80 -Port 443` succeeds.
stages.prompt: Give at least three competing hypotheses and an evidence-driven testing order. Explain what each observation proves and does not prove.
stages.tools: Windows PowerShell (lab only): Resolve-DnsName app.lab.example -Server 10.40.0.53; Test-NetConnection 10.40.0.80 -Port 443. Linux (lab only): dig @10.40.0.53 app.lab.example.
stages.interpret: A DNS timeout can indicate DNS service, route, firewall, or interface failure; successful TCP/443 by IP narrows but does not prove the app works. ICMP alone is insufficient.
criteria: Uses controls or comparisons for hypotheses
Acknowledges limits of ICMP and TCP tests
Keeps all probes inside lab addresses

stages.title: Plan repair and retest
stages.evidence: Switch rollback to host-only restores reachability to DNS, but the name now resolves to 10.40.0.81 instead of expected 10.40.0.80. The application itself answers HTTP 200 on 10.40.0.80.
stages.prompt: Describe two separate faults, their likely owners, the smallest safe fixes, and objective closure criteria.
stages.tools: Snapshot switch config; use internal DNS admin console to review A record; retest name-to-IP resolution and application response after approved correction.
stages.interpret: Network isolation restoration is not the same as correcting a wrong DNS record. Record the initial and final state. Prefer authorized, change-controlled updates.

stages.title: Write the professional incident record
stages.evidence: 14:05 switch change; 14:08 name lookup fails; 14:12 IP-based TCP succeeds; 14:20 host-only restored; 14:25 wrong A record identified; 14:37 corrected and tested.
stages.prompt: Deliver a concise technical timeline, root-cause statement with confidence, impact, prevention, change approval, and retest evidence. Distinguish direct observations from inferences.
stages.tools: Use a structured incident report; export your own lab config and test outputs with timestamps.
stages.interpret: Do not claim the DNS record was changed by the switch operation without evidence. Two faults may be independent.

tracks.title: Identity alert and authorization assessment
tracks.brief: An instructor-generated enterprise log bundle shows an unusually privileged deployment account. You are an authorized read-only analyst. Do not attempt account access, secret extraction, or live role changes.

stages.title: Define hypotheses and evidence
stages.evidence: At 09:00 a deployment ticket is approved. At 09:07 svc-release gets a broad admin role. At 09:12 a successful sign-in appears from an unfamiliar device; the record contains workload identity `pipeline-8`. A different account had a failed sign-in at 09:10.
stages.prompt: Separate observations from assumptions. Give a benign explanation, a malicious explanation, and the minimum corroborating records needed for each.
stages.tools: Review synthetic CSV or JSON sign-in/role logs by identity, timestamp and ticket ID; do not contact live accounts.
stages.interpret: A new device or unusual role is a reason to investigate, not proof of compromise. The failed sign-in from another account is not necessarily related.

stages.title: Reconcile contradictory entries
stages.evidence: Ticket permits role elevation until 09:20. Token issued at 09:08 expires at 10:08. Role-removal event logged 09:21. At 09:35 an API call using the earlier token succeeds on a low-impact endpoint.
stages.prompt: Explain why role removal may not invalidate a previously issued token immediately. Define which token claim, audience and server authorization behaviors need checking.
stages.tools: Inspect fictional JWT header/payload fields without accepting them as verified truth; compare server-side audit records and token expiration. Never paste real secrets into the exercise.
stages.interpret: Claims and expiration are evidence about a token, not automatic proof that the API re-checks current permissions. Revocation semantics depend on implementation.

stages.title: Prioritize containment and prevention
stages.evidence: Account permissions exceed documented deployment needs. No confirmed harmful action exists. Operations requires production continuity.
stages.prompt: Recommend proportional immediate actions, an approved least-privilege redesign and measures to avoid disrupting deployments.
stages.tools: Draft change-control request, permission inventory, temporary credential handling policy and monitoring queries on synthetic logs.
stages.interpret: Do not revoke critical production identity unilaterally; coordinate with account owner and incident responders. Restrict scope, shorten elevation and log approval.

stages.title: Prepare two audiences
stages.evidence: Evidence is incomplete; change records and logs have differing timezones. A manager requests an executive summary and engineers request technical reproduction steps.
stages.prompt: Write an executive summary and a technical appendix. Provide confidence, timeline timezone normalization, evidence gaps, accountable owners and clear success measures.
stages.tools: Use audit log export, a written timeline and risk register; no live assessment required.
stages.interpret: Say 'suspected' when unverified. Keep personally sensitive log data minimized.

tracks.title: Independent enterprise response capstone
tracks.brief: A fictional assessment panel supplies a mixed evidence package: production-like application failures, DNS errors, an automation role change and maintenance activity. The only permitted environment is a local or browser-based simulation, and the capstone tests reasoning and reporting, not offensive access.

stages.title: Triage without a narrative shortcut
stages.evidence: 09:10 maintenance starts; 09:12 automation role expands; 09:14 DNS error rate increases; 09:16 app availability drops; 09:18 storage IO rises. Times are local to two different regions and require normalization.
stages.prompt: List three independent root-cause hypotheses, their expected evidence, a severity rationale and the limits of the event ordering.
stages.tools: Create a timeline in UTC from supplied timezone offsets. Use read-only application, DNS and identity report extracts.
stages.interpret: The displayed ordering cannot establish cause if clocks and timezones differ. Prioritize availability and potential identity misuse without assuming one caused the other.

stages.title: Interpret the supplied measurements
stages.evidence: Of 200 labelled simulated alerts, 20 are true incidents. The detection rule flags 32, of which 12 are true positives. Resolver errors fall to normal after a route rollback, but elevated storage IO remains.
stages.prompt: Calculate precision, recall, false positives and false negatives. Explain why one successful fix does not close the whole incident.
stages.tools: Python on fictional data: tp=12; flagged=32; actual=20; print(tp/flagged,tp/actual,flagged-tp,actual-tp).
stages.interpret: Precision=37.5%, recall=60%, FP=20, FN=8. Storage IO remains a separate signal needing investigation; a DNS fix does not explain everything.
criteria: Does not conflate accuracy and precision
Treats remaining IO as open issue

stages.title: Make a controlled recovery decision
stages.evidence: Rollback option A restores the prior network route but leaves the widened identity role active. Option B revokes the automation role without confirmed credential compromise but may interrupt billing. Option C temporarily reduces application concurrency while preserving logs.
stages.prompt: Rank immediate containment and recovery options under explicit assumptions, and identify what approvals are needed. Give rollback triggers and observability criteria.
stages.tools: Change authorization matrix, snapshot inventory, role ownership list, incident bridge, error-budget dashboard and fictional command outputs.
stages.interpret: There is no universal correct sequence without business criticality and additional evidence. Justify risk trade-offs and make any action reversible where possible.

stages.title: Defend your decision to a reviewer
stages.evidence: An assessor challenges the diagnosis: route rollback normalized DNS but the app still intermittently fails; a deployment token has not expired. No additional tests are permitted.
stages.prompt: Produce an executive report and a technical appendix. State what remains unresolved, the next authorized evidence request, the confidence level of every conclusion, and when you would stop.
stages.tools: Use the supplied fictional evidence only and a clear report structure: scope, observations, inferences, risk, actions, verification, open questions.
stages.interpret: Strong performance includes acknowledging uncertainty, not inventing lab results, resisting pressure to claim complete remediation, and keeping security boundaries intact.
